plain_title: A rare, dangerous reaction to antipsychotic medication
one_liner: A rare emergency reaction to antipsychotics: high fever, severe muscle stiffness, confusion, and unstable pulse or blood pressure.
in_simple_words: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a rare but life-threatening reaction to antipsychotic medication, and occasionally to other drugs that affect dopamine, or to suddenly stopping Parkinson's medication. It usually develops within weeks of starting or increasing a dose. The signs are a high fever, severe muscle stiffness, confusion or reduced consciousness, and a fast or irregular pulse, sweating, or swinging blood pressure. It needs emergency hospital care. With quick treatment most people recover fully.
what_it_can_feel_like: He went stiff and burning hot over two days and we thought it was flu. The ambulance crew knew what it was. He's fine now, on a different medication.
Every psychiatrist since has asked about it. I carry a card in my wallet that says NMS, 2019.
common_signs: High fever with no obvious infection
Severe muscle stiffness, often described as 'lead pipe'
Fast or irregular heartbeat, sweating, blood pressure swings
Usually within weeks of starting or increasing an antipsychotic

myths_vs_facts.myth: It's so rare it isn't worth knowing about.
myths_vs_facts.fact: It's rare, but it can kill, and knowing the signs is what gets people to hospital in time. Everyone on antipsychotics, and their families, should know them.

myths_vs_facts.myth: After NMS you can never take antipsychotics again.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Many people can later restart a different antipsychotic cautiously, under close monitoring, when the benefits are clear.

how_common.plain: NMS affects well under 1 in 100 people taking antipsychotics, with estimates ranging from a tiny fraction of a percent up to a few percent in older studies. Deaths have fallen with better recognition.
how_common.figure: Incidence estimates about 0.02%–3% in reviews; mortality around 5%–12% in recent estimates, down from up to 30% historically
how_common.note: Wide variation; needs a primary citation.

what_helps.plain_summary: NMS is treated in hospital: the medication is stopped, the body is cooled, fluids are given, and the heart, kidneys, and muscles are monitored. Specific medications are sometimes used. Recovery usually takes days to a couple of weeks. Afterwards, the care team reviews whether and how to restart an antipsychotic, usually a different one, at a low dose with close monitoring.
evidence_based_options: Emergency assessment and stopping the triggering medication
Supportive hospital care: cooling, fluids, monitoring
Specific medications in some cases, given in hospital
Careful, monitored reintroduction of a different antipsychotic later, if needed
self_help_that_supports_care: Knowing the warning signs if you or someone you care for takes antipsychotics
Not stopping Parkinson's or antipsychotic medication suddenly without medical advice
Carrying a note of your medications
Telling any new prescriber about a past NMS

when_to_reach_out: If someone taking an antipsychotic develops a high fever with severe stiffness and confusion, call emergency services or go to an emergency department now. Don't wait to see if it passes.
is_not: Fever from an infection, stiffness from ordinary side effects, catatonia, serotonin syndrome, and heatstroke can look similar and are sorted out in hospital.
hope_note: Recognised and treated quickly, most people recover completely and go on to find a medication that suits them.

content_notes: No doses or tapering schedules given; always 'with your prescriber'.
Medical emergency card; crisis strip points to emergency services.
